Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Somalia, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Somalia, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has submitted new evidence in support of his appeal and he is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a positive determination or that the claim be redetermined by a different panel of the RPD.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a different panel. This appeal is allowed. Background and Issue

The Appellant is a citizen of Somalia who made a claim for refugee protection on April 13, 2015. An RPD hearing was held on November 27, 2015. The claim was rejected by the RPD in a decision of December 10, 2015.

A Notice of Appeal was received by the RAD on February 25, 2016 with the appellant's record being perfected on April 22, 2016. The record contained new evidence in the form of a letter from the RPD indicating that there was no complete audio recording of the RPD hearing because the recording device used during the hearing malfunctioned. The issue before the RAD is whether the absence of the audio recording of the hearing amounts to a breach of natural justice. The RAD finds that it does. Appellant's submissions

The Appellant submits that the RPD was only able to produce a 17 minute and 30 second recording of counsel's final submissions at the end of the hearing. The absence of a full recording of the hearing in itself warrants a re-hearing.

These submissions are supported by a letter1 of March 31, 2016 from an RPD case management officer indicating that the recording device used during the hearing malfunctioned and that as a result, there is no complete audio recording of the hearing.

The Appellant relies upon a previous RAD decision in Xe (Re), 2014 CanLII 94325 (CA IRB), in which the RAD found that deficiencies in the CD of the RPD proceeding which made portions of the hearing completely inaudible or incomprehensible were sufficient to find a breach of natural justice and the file was sent back to the RPD for reconsideration. Panel member MacAulay is quoted as follows: The RAD has reviewed the CD found in the RPDR [record], as well as the one that had been provided to the appellant. In the assessment of the RAD, in this particular case both CDs reveal similar problems and that, indeed, portions of the recording are muddled, too quiet or otherwise deficient such that I find the CD to be inadequate for the purpose of either enabling the appellant to properly frame and substantiate the basis of his appeal, or, as well as, precluding the Rad itself from fully reviewing the underlying evidence which the appellant has submitted the RPD has misunderstood, mischaracterized or misconstrued. The RAD must have access to this evidence in order to determine whether the factual conclusions drawn by the RPD are reasonable.

With respect to new evidence, section 110(4) of the IRPA states: 110(4) On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

Clearly the letter from the RPD case management officer meets all of these express statutory requirements because the letter and its contents only arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available before and the Appellant could not have known that he would need it. There is no doubt as to the credibility of the letter. The letter is also central to the RAD's decision. Therefore it is material and relevant. The RPD letter is accepted into evidence on appeal.

As submitted by counsel on appeal, the RPD member, in deciding the case at hand, has relied extensively upon the Appellant's testimony in making negative credibility findings. The RAD finds the RPD impugns the credibility of the Appellant, in fact, concluding that "the claimant has not been credible in his testimony... ".2

The RAD concurs with the Appellant that "Without a fully comprehensible and audible recording of the hearing, the appellant cannot rebut or explain the findings made by the Division member. It is not clear whether the appellant did provide acceptable answers to the Division member's questions. Nor is it possible to know if the Division member misunderstood, misconstrued or mischaracterized evidence provided by the appellant."3

However, it is also submitted that, "Without this information, the lack of a full transcript of the hearing amounts to a breach of natural justice which requires that the matter be referred back to the RPD."4 The RAD finds that while the Appellant may undertake to obtain a transcript of the RPD proceeding, there is no requirement in the RAD Rules for the IRB to provide a written transcript of the RPD proceeding. As such it is not the lack thereof which creates the breach of natural justice, rather, it is the fact that there is no complete audio recording of the proceeding that impairs the Appellant's ability to fully prepare informed pleadings. As a result, the matter must be referred back to the RPD for redetermination.

For the reasons provided above, the RAD allows this appeal and refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a different panel, as per section 111(1)(c) of the IRPA. (signed) "Deborah Morrish" Deborah Morrish October 13, 2016 Date 1 Exhibit P-3, RPD CMO letter of March 31, 2016. 2 Exhibit RPD-1, RPD Reasons and Decision, paragraph 19. 3 Exhibit P-2, Appellant's Record, Memorandum, paragraph 21. 4 Ibid. --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ RAD.25.02 (June 23, 2014) RAD File No. / N° de dossier de la SAR : TB6-12229
